tool.name: Vite
tool.tagline: Fast frontend build tool: instant dev server with HMR and optimized production builds
tool.description: Vite is the build tool behind most new frontend projects: a dev server that serves source files as native ES modules with near-instant hot module replacement, and a production bundler (Rolldown since Vite 8) that outputs optimized, hashed assets. It powers React, Vue, Svelte and Solid apps and frameworks such as Nuxt, SvelteKit, Astro and React Router, and its plugin API is shared by a large ecosystem.

concepts.name: What Vite is and why it is fast
concepts.summary: Vite serves source files as native ES modules in development and bundles them with Rolldown for production.
concepts.why: Understanding Vite's two modes explains nearly every behaviour difference between dev and build.
concepts.body:
Older bundlers such as webpack build the **whole application** into bundles before the dev server can show anything, so start-up and updates slow down as the app grows. **Vite** (French for "fast") splits the problem in two:

- **Development**: the browser loads your code as **native ES modules**. Vite transforms each file on demand when the browser requests it (TypeScript, JSX, Vue SFCs, CSS), so start-up time barely depends on app size. Third-party dependencies are **pre-bundled** once into a few cached files, because packages like lodash-es would otherwise trigger hundreds of requests.
- **Production**: Vite bundles everything with **Rolldown**, a Rust bundler with a Rollup-compatible API (since Vite 8; earlier versions used esbuild plus Rollup), and minifies with Oxc and Lightning CSS. You get tree-shaken, code-split, content-hashed files.

On top of that, **hot module replacement (HMR)** swaps edited modules into the running page, preserving state, typically in milliseconds.

Start a project with `npm create vite@latest`, choosing a template (vanilla, React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, Lit, Preact, Qwik, each with or without TypeScript). Vite 8 requires Node 20.19+ or 22.12+.

Because dev and build use different pipelines, always test the production build (`vite build` then `vite preview`) before deploying.
concepts.code:
npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react-ts
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev
#   VITE v8.x  ready in 300 ms
#   ➜  Local:   http://localhost:5173/

npm run build      # vite build -> dist/
npm run preview    # serve dist/ locally on http://localhost:4173
takeaways: Dev: native ESM, files transformed on demand
Dependencies are pre-bundled and cached
Production: bundled with Rolldown, minified with Oxc
Always check `vite build` + `vite preview` before deploying
pitfalls: Assuming dev behaviour proves production works; the pipelines differ.

quiz.q: Why does Vite's dev server start quickly even for large apps?
options: It caches the final bundle on disk
It serves source as native ES modules and transforms files on demand
quiz.explain: No full bundle is built up front; the browser requests modules and Vite transforms each one when asked.

concepts.name: Project structure and the CLI
concepts.summary: Know why index.html is the entry point, what lives in public/ versus src/, and the dev, build and preview commands.
concepts.why: Vite's conventions differ from older tools, and knowing them avoids broken paths.
concepts.body:
In a Vite project, **`index.html` is the entry point** and sits at the project root, not in `public/`. Vite reads it, follows `<script type="module" src="/src/main.ts">`, and builds the module graph from there. During build it rewrites the HTML with hashed asset URLs. Multi-page apps simply have several HTML files.

Typical layout:

- `index.html`: entry; may reference `/src/...` paths, which are resolved from the project root.
- `src/`: your code and imported assets. Anything imported is processed, hashed and tree-shaken.
- `public/`: files copied **as-is** to the output root, served at `/`. Use it for `robots.txt`, `favicon.ico` or files that must keep exact names. Reference them with absolute paths (`/robots.txt`) and never import them.
- `vite.config.ts` (optional): configuration.

The CLI:

- `vite` (or `vite dev`): dev server on port 5173, `--host` to expose it on your network, `--open` to launch a browser.
- `vite build`: production build into `dist/`.
- `vite preview`: serve `dist/` locally on port 4173. Not a production server.

Scripts in `package.json` usually map `dev`, `build` and `preview` to these. For TypeScript projects, templates run `tsc -b` before `vite build`, because Vite only **strips** types and never type-checks.
concepts.code:
my-app/
├── index.html            # entry point (at the root!)
├── public/
│   └── robots.txt        # copied as-is -> /robots.txt
├── src/
│   ├── main.ts           # <script type="module" src="/src/main.ts">
│   ├── App.tsx
│   └── assets/logo.svg   # imported -> processed and hashed
├── vite.config.ts
└── package.json
    "scripts": {
      "dev": "vite",
      "build": "tsc -b && vite build",   // Vite strips types, tsc checks them
      "preview": "vite preview"
    }
takeaways: index.html at the root is the entry point
Imported files are processed; public/ files are copied verbatim
dev on 5173, preview on 4173
Vite strips TypeScript types but never type-checks
pitfalls: Importing files from public/, which bypasses hashing and breaks with a non-root `base`.

quiz.q: Where should a file live if it must be served at exactly `/robots.txt`, unprocessed?
quiz.explain: public/ files are copied to the output root without hashing or transformation.

concepts.name: Importing CSS and static assets
concepts.summary: Import CSS, CSS modules and preprocessors directly, and turn images, fonts and text files into URLs or strings with query suffixes.
concepts.why: Vite treats styles and assets as part of the module graph, which changes how you reference them.
concepts.body:
In Vite, CSS and assets are **imported from JavaScript**, and the build takes care of the rest.

**CSS**:

- `import "./style.css"` injects the styles (with HMR in dev) and extracts them into a hashed `.css` file in production.
- Files named `*.module.css` are **CSS modules**: `import styles from "./card.module.css"` gives an object of locally scoped class names.
- Sass, Less and Stylus work after installing the preprocessor (`npm i -D sass-embedded`). PostCSS config is picked up automatically, and Lightning CSS handles minification and syntax lowering.

**Assets**:

- `import logoUrl from "./logo.svg"` returns a URL string. Small assets (under 4 KB by default, `build.assetsInlineLimit`) are inlined as data URIs; larger ones get hashed filenames like `logo-Bx3k9.svg`.
- Query suffixes change what you get: `?url` (always a URL), `?raw` (file contents as a string), `?inline` (data URI), `?worker` (a Web Worker constructor).
- `new URL("./img.png", import.meta.url)` also works for dynamic asset paths, as long as the path is statically analyzable.
- `import data from "./data.json"` works too, including named imports of top-level fields.

Referencing assets in CSS (`url(./bg.png)`) and in `index.html` is rewritten the same way.
takeaways: Import CSS from JS; `*.module.css` gives scoped class names
Imported assets become hashed URLs or inline data URIs
Suffixes: ?url, ?raw, ?inline, ?worker
Preprocessors work once installed, no config needed
pitfalls: Building asset paths with string concatenation at runtime, which the bundler cannot see or hash.

quiz.q: What does `import text from './notes.txt?raw'` give you?
options: The file's contents as a string
quiz.explain: `?raw` imports the file contents as a string.

concepts.name: Environment variables and modes
concepts.summary: Expose VITE_-prefixed variables via import.meta.env, load .env files per mode, and keep secrets out of the client bundle.
concepts.why: Every app needs per-environment configuration, and leaking a secret into the bundle is a classic mistake.
concepts.body:
Vite exposes environment information on `import.meta.env`:

- Built-ins: `MODE` (`development`, `production` or your custom mode), `DEV`, `PROD`, `SSR`, `BASE_URL`.
- Your variables, **only if prefixed with `VITE_`**: `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`. Others (like `DB_PASSWORD`) are not exposed, by design.

Values come from `.env` files in the project root, loaded in this order with later ones winning:

- `.env` (always), `.env.local` (always, git-ignored)
- `.env.[mode]`, `.env.[mode].local`

Variables already set in the shell have the highest priority: `VITE_API_URL=... vite build`.

The **mode** defaults to `development` for `vite` and `production` for `vite build`; choose another with `--mode staging`, which loads `.env.staging`. Mode is separate from `NODE_ENV`.

Everything exposed is **inlined into the JavaScript at build time** as a string. That means:

- Never put secrets in `VITE_` variables: anyone can read them in the bundle.
- Values are strings; convert `"true"` or `"3"` yourself.
- Changing a variable requires a rebuild, not just a redeploy. For runtime configuration, fetch a `config.json` at start-up instead.

Inside `vite.config.ts`, `.env` files are not loaded automatically; use `loadEnv(mode, process.cwd())` if config needs them.
concepts.code:
# .env
VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com
DB_PASSWORD=hunter2            # NOT exposed: no VITE_ prefix

# .env.staging
VITE_API_URL=https://staging-api.example.com

// src/api.js
console.log(import.meta.env.MODE);          // "development" | "production" | "staging"
console.log(import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL);  // inlined at build time
console.log(import.meta.env.DB_PASSWORD);   // undefined
const debug = import.meta.env.VITE_DEBUG === "true"; // values are strings

# build for staging
npx vite build --mode staging
takeaways: Only `VITE_`-prefixed variables reach client code
`.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.[mode]`, `.env.[mode].local`; shell wins
Values are inlined at build time as strings
Never put secrets in VITE_ variables
pitfalls: Storing an API secret in VITE_STRIPE_SECRET and shipping it to every browser.

quiz.q: Why can't a `VITE_` variable be changed by restarting the deployed static site?
options: Vite caches it in the browser
Its value is inlined into the bundle at build time
quiz.explain: Vite replaces import.meta.env.VITE_* with literal values during the build.

concepts.name: Configuration and the dev server
concepts.summary: Write vite.config with defineConfig, add path aliases, and configure the dev server's port, host and API proxy.
concepts.why: Most real projects need aliases and a proxy to talk to their backend during development.
concepts.body:
`vite.config.ts` (or `.js`/`.mjs`) exports a config object, ideally wrapped in `defineConfig` for type hints. It can also export a function receiving `{ command, mode }` to vary settings between `serve` and `build`.

Frequently used options:

- `plugins`: framework and feature plugins, e.g. `react()`.
- `resolve.alias`: map `@` to `src/` so imports become `@/components/Button`. Mirror it in `tsconfig.json` `paths` for TypeScript (or use the `resolve.tsconfigPaths` option / a plugin).
- `base`: the public path when the app is deployed under a sub-path, e.g. `/docs/`.
- `server.port`, `server.host` (`true` to listen on all addresses), `server.open`, `server.strictPort`.
- `server.proxy`: forward API calls to your backend, avoiding CORS in development. `changeOrigin: true` rewrites the `Host` header; `rewrite` adjusts paths; `ws: true` proxies WebSockets.
- `server.allowedHosts`: hosts other than localhost (for tunnels or containers) must be listed.
- `build.outDir`, `build.sourcemap`, and `preview` options that mirror `server`.

Vite restarts the dev server automatically when the config file changes. The dev server is for development only: it is not hardened and should never be exposed to the internet.
takeaways: `defineConfig` gives typed config; a function form sees command and mode
Aliases need matching tsconfig paths
`server.proxy` forwards API calls and avoids CORS in dev
Set `base` when deploying under a sub-path
pitfalls: Exposing the dev server publicly as if it were a production server.

quiz.q: What does a `server.proxy` entry for `/api` solve during development?
options: Calling the backend from the same origin, avoiding CORS issues
quiz.explain: The dev server forwards matching requests to the backend, so the browser sees one origin.

concepts.name: Hot module replacement
concepts.summary: See how HMR swaps changed modules over a WebSocket, what HMR boundaries are, and use the import.meta.hot API.
concepts.why: Knowing when HMR applies versus full reloads explains lost state and stale modules during development.
concepts.body:
When you save a file, the dev server finds the changed module in its **module graph** and walks up the importers looking for an **HMR boundary**: a module that has declared it can accept updates. It then sends a message over a WebSocket, and the client re-imports the new version of the changed modules, without reloading the page.

- Framework plugins make components boundaries automatically: React Fast Refresh (`@vitejs/plugin-react`), Vue, Svelte and Solid preserve component state across edits.
- CSS updates are swapped in place.
- If no boundary is found up to the entry, Vite does a **full page reload**.

The **`import.meta.hot`** API lets plain modules opt in:

- `import.meta.hot.accept(cb)`: accept updates of this module; `cb` receives the new module.
- `import.meta.hot.dispose(cb)`: clean up side effects (timers, listeners) before the old module is replaced.
- `import.meta.hot.data`: persist state between versions.
- `import.meta.hot.invalidate()`: give up and propagate to importers.

Always guard with `if (import.meta.hot)`; the code is removed from production builds.

Gotchas: React Fast Refresh only works when a file exports only components (mixed exports cause full reloads); modules with side effects such as global listeners need `dispose`; HMR over Docker or WSL may need `server.watch.usePolling` or `server.hmr` settings.
takeaways: HMR walks up importers to the nearest accepting boundary
No boundary found means a full page reload
`accept`, `dispose`, `data`, `invalidate` on import.meta.hot
Guard with `if (import.meta.hot)`; stripped in production
pitfalls: Exporting constants and components from the same React file, which breaks Fast Refresh.

quiz.q: A changed module and all its importers up to the entry have no HMR boundary. What happens?
quiz.explain: Without an accepting boundary, Vite falls back to reloading the page.

concepts.name: Production builds and deployment
concepts.summary: Build with vite build, understand hashed output and code splitting, set browser targets and base, and deploy dist/ as static files.
concepts.why: The build output is what users actually download.
concepts.body:
`vite build` produces a static `dist/` folder: the rewritten `index.html`, and `assets/` with **content-hashed** JS, CSS and asset files (`index-D0ftifMV.js`). Hashes change only when content changes, so you can serve `assets/` with long-lived immutable caching and only `index.html` with no-cache.

What happens during the build:

- **Bundling and tree-shaking** with Rolldown; unused exports are dropped.
- **Code splitting**: each dynamic `import()` becomes a separate chunk loaded on demand. Shared modules are extracted into common chunks, and Vite preloads a chunk's dependencies in parallel.
- **Minification** with Oxc (JS) and Lightning CSS (CSS). CSS is extracted per chunk.
- **Syntax lowering** to `build.target`, by default `'baseline-widely-available'` (browsers that have supported a feature for about 30 months). Vite does not add polyfills; use `@vitejs/plugin-legacy` for old browsers.

Useful options: `build.sourcemap` (`true`, or `'hidden'` to upload to an error tracker without exposing them), `build.outDir`, `build.assetsInlineLimit`, and `build.chunkSizeWarningLimit` (the "chunk larger than 500 kB" warning).

Deploy `dist/` to any static host (Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages, GitHub Pages, S3 + CDN, Nginx). For client-side routers, configure the host to fall back to `index.html` for unknown paths. If the app lives under a sub-path, set `base`.
takeaways: Output is static: hashed assets plus index.html
Dynamic `import()` creates on-demand chunks
Default target is baseline-widely-available; no automatic polyfills
Cache assets forever, never cache index.html
pitfalls: Caching index.html for a long time, so users keep loading old asset hashes after a deploy.

quiz.q: Why can files in dist/assets be cached for a year?
options: Their names contain content hashes, so changed content gets a new URL
quiz.explain: Content hashing makes every changed file a new URL, so old URLs are immutable.

concepts.name: Using plugins and framework integrations
concepts.summary: Add official and community plugins, control their order and when they apply, and know that Vite plugins extend the Rollup plugin interface.
concepts.why: Framework support, legacy browsers, PWAs and much more come from plugins.
concepts.body:
Vite itself handles JS, TS, CSS and assets; everything else is a **plugin** in the `plugins` array.

- Official plugins: `@vitejs/plugin-react` (Fast Refresh, JSX), `@vitejs/plugin-react-swc`, `@vitejs/plugin-vue`, `@vitejs/plugin-vue-jsx`, `@vitejs/plugin-legacy`. Svelte, Solid, Preact and Qwik maintain their own.
- Community plugins cover PWAs, SVG-as-component, image optimization, bundle visualizers, and more.

Vite plugins are a **superset of the Rollup plugin interface**, so many Rollup (and Rolldown) plugins work unchanged. Vite-specific hooks add dev-server and HTML integration.

Controlling plugins:

- `enforce: "pre" | "post"` changes ordering relative to Vite's core plugins (e.g. a plugin that must see raw source runs `pre`).
- `apply: "serve" | "build"` (or a function) limits a plugin to dev or build.
- Arrays are flattened, and falsy entries are ignored, so `mode === "analyze" && visualizer()` works.

Frameworks such as Nuxt, SvelteKit, Astro, React Router (framework mode), TanStack Start and Vike are themselves Vite plugins plus conventions. Frameworks often configure Vite for you, so check their config hooks before adding plugins directly.

Keep the list short: each plugin runs on every transformed module, and slow plugins are a common cause of slow dev servers.
takeaways: Plugins add frameworks and features; Vite plugins extend Rollup's interface
`enforce` orders plugins, `apply` limits them to dev or build
Falsy entries in `plugins` are ignored
Meta-frameworks are Vite plugins with conventions
pitfalls: Stacking many heavy plugins and blaming Vite for slow transforms.

quiz.q: How do you make a plugin run only for `vite build`?
options: Put it last in the array
quiz.explain: `apply` restricts a plugin to the serve or build command.

concepts.name: Dependency pre-bundling
concepts.summary: Understand why Vite pre-bundles node_modules, how the cache works, and fix issues with optimizeDeps include and exclude.
concepts.why: Most 'works after restart' and 'duplicate React' dev issues trace back to dependency optimization.
concepts.body:
On the first dev-server start, Vite scans your source for bare imports (`import { debounce } from "lodash-es"`) and **pre-bundles** those dependencies (using Rolldown in Vite 8) into `node_modules/.vite/deps`. Two reasons:

- **CommonJS and UMD to ESM**: many packages still ship CommonJS, which browsers cannot import natively.
- **Fewer requests**: a package made of hundreds of internal modules becomes one file, avoiding request waterfalls.

The browser then receives cached, strongly cached (`max-age=31536000,immutable`) files, and Vite rewrites your imports to point at them.

The cache is invalidated when the lockfile, the relevant config or `patchedDependencies` change. Force a rebuild with `vite --force`, or delete `node_modules/.vite`.

When something goes wrong:

- **Dependency discovered late**: an import that only appears after navigation (e.g. inside a lazily loaded route) triggers re-optimization and a page reload. Add it to `optimizeDeps.include`.
- **Linked monorepo packages** are treated as source, not pre-bundled. If such a package ships CommonJS, add it to `include`.
- **Large ESM-only packages** that are already browser-ready can go in `optimizeDeps.exclude`.
- **Duplicated singletons** (two copies of React) usually need `resolve.dedupe: ["react", "react-dom"]`.

Pre-bundling applies only to the dev server; production builds bundle dependencies along with your code.
takeaways: Pre-bundling converts CommonJS to ESM and collapses many files
Cache lives in node_modules/.vite; `--force` rebuilds it
`include` late or linked CJS deps; `exclude` browser-ready ESM
Use `resolve.dedupe` for duplicated singletons
pitfalls: Repeatedly deleting node_modules instead of adding a late-discovered dependency to `optimizeDeps.include`.

quiz.q: Navigating to a lazy route causes 'new dependencies optimized, reloading'. What is the fix?
quiz.explain: Including it up front lets Vite pre-bundle it at start-up instead of mid-session.

concepts.name: Library mode
concepts.summary: Build a publishable package with build.lib: entry, formats, file names, and externalized dependencies, plus types and exports.
concepts.why: Component libraries and SDKs need different output than apps.
concepts.body:
An app build produces an HTML entry and hashed assets. A **library** needs stable file names, ESM (and sometimes CommonJS) output, and must **not** bundle its dependencies. Vite's **library mode** handles this:

- `build.lib.entry`: one or more entry files (an object for multiple entry points).
- `build.lib.formats`: defaults to `['es', 'umd']` for a single entry; `['es', 'cjs']` is common for npm packages. `name` is required for `umd`/`iife` (the global variable).
- `build.lib.fileName`: base name for output files.
- `build.rolldownOptions.external`: dependencies and peer dependencies that consumers install, e.g. `react`, `react/jsx-runtime`. Otherwise you ship a second copy of React inside your package.

What Vite does not do for you:

- **Type declarations**: run `tsc --emitDeclarationOnly` or a plugin such as `vite-plugin-dts`.
- **package.json**: point `exports` (with `types`, `import`, `require` conditions) at the generated files and list them in `files`.
- CSS is emitted as a separate file that consumers must import; document it.

For pure TypeScript libraries without CSS or framework transforms, dedicated tools (tsdown, built on Rolldown, or plain `tsc`) are often simpler. Library mode shines for component libraries that need Vite's CSS and framework plugins.
takeaways: `build.lib` sets entry, formats and file names
Externalize dependencies and peer dependencies
Generate .d.ts separately; wire `exports` and `files` yourself
Consider tsdown or tsc for plain TypeScript libraries
pitfalls: Forgetting to externalize React in a component library, shipping a second React copy.

quiz.q: Why mark `react` as external in a React component library build?
options: So the consumer's single React instance is used instead of a bundled copy
quiz.explain: Bundling React would create a second instance and break hooks.

concepts.name: Writing Vite plugins
concepts.summary: Implement resolveId, load and transform hooks, virtual modules, and Vite-specific hooks like configureServer and transformIndexHtml.
concepts.why: Custom plugins solve code generation, integrations and build-time transforms that no config option covers.
concepts.body:
A plugin is an object with a `name` and hook functions, usually returned from a factory so it can take options.

**Rollup-compatible hooks** (run in dev and build):

- `resolveId(source, importer)`: map an import specifier to an id. Returning an id prefixed with `\0` marks it as **virtual** so other plugins leave it alone.
- `load(id)`: return the code for an id, e.g. generated source for a virtual module.
- `transform(code, id)`: modify a module's code; return `{ code, map }` with a source map when possible. Use **hook filters** (`transform: { filter: { id: /\.md$/ }, handler }`) so the native bundler can skip calling into JavaScript for irrelevant files, a big speed win with Rolldown.
- `buildStart`, `generateBundle` and other build hooks.

**Vite-specific hooks**:

- `config` / `configResolved`: modify or read the final config.
- `configureServer(server)`: add dev-server middleware (`server.middlewares.use`) or watch extra files.
- `transformIndexHtml`: inject tags into `index.html`.
- `hotUpdate`: customize HMR for certain files.

By convention, virtual module ids start with `virtual:` in user-facing imports. Name plugins `vite-plugin-*` (or `rolldown-plugin-*` if bundler-agnostic). Debug with `vite-plugin-inspect`, which shows every transform step per module.
takeaways: resolveId + load create virtual modules (`\0` prefix)
transform rewrites code; return source maps
Hook filters let Rolldown skip JS calls for irrelevant files
Vite-only hooks: configureServer, transformIndexHtml, hotUpdate
pitfalls: Transforming every file with a regex check inside the hook instead of a hook filter.

quiz.q: Why do virtual module ids returned from resolveId start with `\0`?
options: It tells other plugins and the file system that this is not a real file
quiz.explain: The null-byte prefix is the Rollup convention for ids that other plugins should not process.

concepts.name: SSR and the Environment API
concepts.summary: Render on the server with Vite in middleware mode, build client and server bundles, and understand environments and module runners.
concepts.why: Frameworks with server rendering are built on these APIs, and debugging them requires understanding them.
concepts.body:
For **server-side rendering**, the server must execute your app code (JSX, TS, CSS imports) in Node. Vite supports this in two phases:

**Development**: create the Vite server in **middleware mode** inside your own Node server (Express, Hono, etc.). For each request, load the server entry through Vite, which transforms it on the fly with HMR, render HTML, and pass it through `vite.transformIndexHtml` so client scripts and HMR are injected. The classic API is `vite.ssrLoadModule(url)`.

**Production**: build twice, `vite build` for the client and `vite build --ssr src/entry-server.js` for the server, then import the server bundle directly with no Vite at runtime. `ssr.noExternal` controls which dependencies are bundled into the server build; by default node_modules stay external.

The **Environment API** (introduced in Vite 6, evolving since) generalizes this. A Vite server or build now has several named **environments**, by default `client` and `ssr`, each with its own module graph, resolve conditions and plugin pipeline. Custom environments target edge runtimes or workers. Code runs in an environment through a **module runner**, which can live in the same Node process or in another runtime (workerd, Deno). Frameworks use this to run server code in a production-like runtime during development.

Application authors rarely touch these APIs directly; they come through frameworks. Plugin authors must be environment-aware (e.g. `this.environment` in hooks).
takeaways: Dev SSR: Vite in middleware mode loads server code with HMR
Prod SSR: separate client and --ssr builds, no Vite at runtime
Environments: client, ssr and custom, each with its own module graph
Module runners execute environment code, possibly in other runtimes
pitfalls: Shipping the dev middleware setup to production instead of the built server bundle.

quiz.q: What does the Environment API add over the classic SSR setup?
options: Multiple named environments with their own module graphs and runtimes
quiz.explain: It generalizes client/ssr into configurable environments executed through module runners.

concepts.name: Rolldown, chunking and performance
concepts.summary: Know what changed with Rolldown and Oxc in Vite 8, control chunking with codeSplitting groups, and diagnose slow dev servers and large bundles.
concepts.why: Large apps hit slow cold starts and oversized bundles; fixing them needs knowledge of the toolchain.
concepts.body:
**Vite 8** replaced the esbuild + Rollup pair with **Rolldown** (bundler) and **Oxc** (parser, transformer, minifier), both written in Rust by the VoidZero team. One toolchain for dev pre-bundling and production means more consistent behaviour and much faster builds. Config moved accordingly: `build.rolldownOptions` replaces `build.rollupOptions` (still accepted as a deprecated alias), and the `oxc` option replaces `esbuild`.

**Chunking**: by default, Rolldown creates one chunk per entry and per dynamic import, plus shared chunks. To group modules yourself, use `output.codeSplitting.groups`, each with a `name` and a `test` (regex or function), plus optional size limits like `minSize`, `maxSize` and `priority`. The Rollup-era `manualChunks` function still works but is deprecated. Splitting vendor code into stable chunks improves cache hit rates across deploys; splitting too much causes request waterfalls.

**Dev server performance**:

- Audit slow plugins: `vite --debug plugin-transform` or `vite-plugin-inspect`.
- Avoid **barrel files** (`index.ts` re-exporting hundreds of modules): every import loads them all.
- Use explicit file extensions in imports to reduce resolution work, and `server.warmup.clientFiles` to pre-transform frequently used files.

**Bundle analysis**: `rollup-plugin-visualizer` or `vite-bundle-analyzer`, then replace heavy dependencies, lazy-load routes, and check that tree-shaking works (`sideEffects: false` in packages).
takeaways: Vite 8: Rolldown + Oxc; rolldownOptions and oxc replace rollupOptions and esbuild
`codeSplitting.groups` controls chunks; manualChunks is deprecated
